concepts.title: Ocean Zones
concepts.contentHtml:
The ocean is layered. The top ~200 m — the photic zone — gets enough sunlight for photosynthesis. Below 200 m: aphotic zone, where life relies on detritus from above (or chemosynthesis at hydrothermal vents).

Deeper still: bathyal (200-2000 m), abyssal (2000-6000 m), and hadal (>6000 m). Pressure rises 1 atm per 10 m. Temperature drops to ~2-4 °C in the deep.

Most ocean volume is dark, cold, and high-pressure. The abyss covers ~60% of Earth's surface area — by far the planet's largest habitat.

concepts.title: Plankton — The Foundation
concepts.contentHtml:
Plankton drift with currents. Phytoplankton (cyanobacteria, diatoms, coccolithophores, dinoflagellates) photosynthesize and form the base of the marine food web. Zooplankton (copepods, krill, larvae of larger animals) graze them.

Marine photosynthesis fixes ~50 Gt C/year — comparable to land photosynthesis. Tiny Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus cyanobacteria alone account for a major slice.

Plankton biomass turns over fast — most of it is recycled within days. The 'biological pump' carries some carbon to the deep ocean for centuries.

concepts.title: From Plankton to Whales
concepts.contentHtml:
The marine food web has more trophic levels than most terrestrial ones. Phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → bigger fish → top predators (tuna, sharks, marine mammals).

Some giants short-circuit the chain: blue whales filter krill directly. Whale sharks and basking sharks eat plankton. Manta rays. Filter-feeding bypasses several trophic levels and supports enormous body sizes.

Bottom-up food limits and top-down predator control both shape marine ecosystems. Overfishing of top predators has cascading effects (often unfavorable) throughout the web.

concepts.title: What Is a Coral?
concepts.contentHtml:
Coral colonies are made of tiny polyps — relatives of jellyfish and anemones — that secrete calcium carbonate skeletons. Reef-building corals harbor symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) inside their tissues.

The algae photosynthesize, providing sugars to the coral. The coral provides shelter and nitrogenous waste. This symbiosis is the engine of reef productivity — and its weak point.

concepts.title: Reef Diversity
concepts.contentHtml:
Coral reefs cover <0.1% of ocean area but harbor 25% of all marine species. Fish, crustaceans, mollusks, sponges, urchins, cleaning shrimp, octopuses — biological wealth concentrated.

Reef structure (the 3D matrix of coral skeletons) creates microhabitats for thousands of species. Productivity rivals tropical rainforests.

Worth ~$10 trillion annually in tourism, fisheries, and coastline protection. Half a billion people depend directly on reef resources.

concepts.title: Reef Crisis
concepts.contentHtml:
Warming oceans cause coral bleaching — heat-stressed corals expel their zooxanthellae and turn white. Without the algae, they slowly starve.

The Great Barrier Reef has had repeated mass bleaching events since 2016. About half of all reef-building corals have been lost since the 1950s.

Ocean acidification (CO₂ → carbonic acid) makes carbonate skeletons harder to build. Combined with overfishing, runoff, and disease, reefs are perhaps the most threatened major ecosystem on Earth.

concepts.title: Hydrothermal Vents
concepts.contentHtml:
At mid-ocean ridges, seawater seeps into hot crust, gets heated to >300 °C, dissolves minerals, and erupts back as 'black smokers'. Discovered in 1977 — these vent systems shocked biologists.

The communities around them — giant tube worms, vent shrimp, mussels, crabs — don't depend on sunlight. They depend on chemosynthesis: bacteria oxidize H₂S from vent fluids to produce energy and biomass.

Tube worms (Riftia) host these bacteria internally — they have no mouth or gut, just a chemosynthetic symbiosis.

concepts.title: Adaptations to Pressure & Cold
concepts.contentHtml:
Deep-sea organisms have specialized lipids that stay fluid at high pressure. Their proteins are stabilized by piezolytes (osmolytes that counteract pressure denaturation). Some retain larval features (paedomorphosis).

Anglerfish have lure organs with luminescent bacteria. Many deep fish have huge eyes (catching faint photons of bioluminescence) or no eyes at all. Some have transparent bodies.

Bioluminescence is the rule rather than the exception in the open deep sea — a way to find prey, mates, or distract predators.

concepts.title: Origin of Life and Vents
concepts.contentHtml:
Hydrothermal vents have inspired theories about life's origin. The chemical disequilibria, mineral surfaces, and continual energy flow plausibly fostered the first replicators.

Mike Russell and Bill Martin's alkaline vent hypothesis places life's origin at less-extreme alkaline vents (Lost City type), where thermodynamic gradients across mineral 'cell-like' compartments could power early metabolism.

Vents may also exist on icy moons (Europa, Enceladus) — making them prime targets for astrobiology.

title: Marine Vertebrates
description: Fish, sharks, mammals, and the return to the sea

concepts.title: Fish Diversity
concepts.contentHtml:
Fish are the most species-rich vertebrate group — over 30,000 species of bony fish (Osteichthyes) plus a thousand-odd cartilaginous fish (sharks, rays, chimaeras).

Adaptations are stunning: ice fish with antifreeze proteins; mudskippers that walk on land; deep-sea anglers with lure-tipped fishing rods; electric eels that stun prey with hundreds of volts.

Modern fishing has reshaped fish populations. Many large predatory fish (cod, tuna) are at small fractions of historical biomass. Recovery in well-managed fisheries shows sustainable harvest is possible — but requires real management.

concepts.title: Marine Mammals
concepts.contentHtml:
Whales, dolphins, seals, sea cows — all are mammals that returned to the sea. Cetaceans (whales/dolphins) descended from artiodactyls (cow/hippo relatives) ~50 Mya. Pinnipeds (seals) from bear-like ancestors more recently.

Adaptations: streamlined body, modified limbs, specialized respiration (whales hold breath for >2 hours), echolocation in toothed whales, blubber for thermal insulation.

Blue whales are the largest animals ever to have lived (~30 m, ~150 tonnes). Dependence on krill at the bottom of the food chain lets them grow this big.

concepts.title: Migration and Navigation
concepts.contentHtml:
Many marine animals migrate enormous distances. Arctic terns migrate from pole to pole annually (~70,000 km). Salmon return from oceans to natal streams to spawn. Sea turtles cross entire ocean basins.

Navigation cues: Earth's magnetic field, position of sun and stars, ocean currents and temperatures, smells (especially for salmon).

Migrations are vulnerable to many disturbances — fishing nets, climate-driven shifts in prey distribution, light pollution disorientating sea turtle hatchlings.

concepts.title: Ocean Warming and Acidification
concepts.contentHtml:
The ocean has absorbed ~90% of excess heat from human emissions. Sea-surface temperatures have risen ~1 °C since pre-industrial. The ocean has also taken up ~30% of anthropogenic CO₂, lowering pH by ~0.1 (a 26% increase in [H⁺]).

Warming drives bleaching, range shifts, and ocean stratification (less mixing → less nutrient supply to surface). Acidification weakens shells and reef-building corals.

Both are accelerating. Even rapid emission cuts will not fully reverse them on human timescales — but they limit how much worse it gets.

concepts.title: Plastic and Pollution
concepts.contentHtml:
~10 million tonnes of plastic enter the ocean each year. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch concentrates plastic; microplastics permeate everything. Ingested plastic kills seabirds, turtles, whales.

Chemical pollution (PCBs, heavy metals, oil spills) and nutrient runoff (causing dead zones via eutrophication) compound the threats. The Gulf of Mexico's hypoxic dead zone is ~14,000 km² seasonally.

Each impact has solutions — but solutions need political will, infrastructure, and global cooperation, often against entrenched economic interests.

concepts.title: Conservation Successes & MPAs
concepts.contentHtml:
Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) restrict fishing and exploitation. Well-managed MPAs see fish biomass recover 3-5× over decades. As of 2024, ~8% of the ocean is in some MPA — the global target is 30% by 2030 (the '30x30' initiative).

Whale populations are recovering since the 1986 commercial whaling moratorium. Sea otters are returning to North Pacific kelp forests. Some fisheries (Norwegian cod, US scallops) have been restored.

Restoration is possible. Decline is not destiny. The challenge is acting fast enough on a global scale.
